nameStory: The "many-fruited" part of this lichen's name comes from its tendency to produce numerous finger-like reproductive structures called apothecia along its edges. "Pelt" refers to its leathery, skin-like appearance that resembles an animal hide spread flat on the ground. The scientific name "polydactylon" literally means "many fingers," referring to those abundant fruiting bodies that look like tiny digits reaching outward.
description: Many-fruited pelt lichen is a large, leafy lichen that spreads across the ground like a leathery mat. It forms broad, flat lobes that can span several inches across, with a distinctive blue-green to gray-green color when moist. The underside is pale with a network of dark veins, and the edges are often decorated with multiple brown, finger-like fruiting structures. This is one of the more substantial lichens you'll encounter, sometimes reaching 6-8 inches across in mature specimens.

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Look for multiple brown, finger-like apothecia (fruiting bodies) along the lobe edges - they feel firm and slightly spongy when fresh, like tiny brown hot dogs attached to the lichen's rim

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms large, flat, leafy lobes that lie against the substrate like pieces of thick, flexible leather - you can often lift and bend the edges without breaking them

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Blue-green to gray-green when wet, becoming more brownish or olive when dry - the color change is quite dramatic after rain

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Upper surface feels smooth to slightly rough, like well-worn leather, without the powdery soredia or bumpy isidia found on many other lichens

idTips.label: Underside Features
idTips.description: Pale underside with prominent dark veins that feel slightly raised - like looking at the back of a leaf with very pronounced venation

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: One of the larger pelt lichens, often 4-8 inches across when fully developed, making it hard to miss when present

habitat: Found on moss-covered soil, rotting logs, and among vegetation in moist, shaded areas throughout New England's forests. Prefers areas with consistent moisture like stream banks, north-facing slopes, and the mossy floor of mature deciduous and mixed woods. Often grows alongside other large lichens and bryophytes in rich, organic soils.

seasonality.spring: Most vibrant after spring rains when the blue-green colors are at their brightest. Fresh growth may be visible at lobe tips, and reproductive structures are often most prominent.
seasonality.summer: May appear more subdued and brownish during dry periods, but becomes dramatically colorful after summer storms. Look for it in consistently moist microhabitats.
seasonality.fall: Colors remain visible as deciduous leaves fall, making it easier to spot on the increasingly bare forest floor. Often looks refreshed by fall rains.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible under light snow cover and shows excellent color during winter thaws. One of the few colorful things you'll find on the forest floor in winter.

funFact: This lichen is essentially a living partnership between a fungus and blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) that can actually pull nitrogen right out of the air and turn it into plant food - making it a natural fertilizer factory that enriches the forest soil wherever it grows.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other large pelt lichens, but the "many-fruited" clue is in the name - count those brown finger-like fruiting bodies along the edges. If you see numerous apothecia (more than 2-3 per lobe), you're likely looking at polydactylon rather than its relatives.
contextualKnowledge: The pelt lichen family gets its name from the resemblance to animal pelts, but don't let that fool you into thinking they're related to animals - they're actually closer to mushrooms than to anything furry. Many field guides focus heavily on microscopic features for pelt lichen identification, but the number and arrangement of fruiting structures can often be determined with just a hand lens.
compareHints: Distinguished from dog pelt lichen by having many more fruiting structures along the edges rather than just a few large ones. Unlike freckled pelt lichen, it lacks the distinctive white spots (cephalodia) on the upper surface. The abundant apothecia set it apart from most other pelt lichens, which typically have fewer, more scattered reproductive structures.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the pelt lichens, scaly pelt is the only one in New England with prominent phyllidia scattered across its surface.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, horizontal pelt lichen is unique for its completely prostrate growth habit - it never curls up at the edges like dog pelt lichen or forms the ruffled, frilly margins of freckled pelt lichen.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, dog pelt lichen stands out for its preference for growing directly on soil rather than trees, and its particularly well-defined dark veining on a pale underside.
Among the pelt lichens, ruffled freckled pelt stands out for its notably bumpy, textured surface and strongly ruffled edges.
Unlike all other pelt lichens in New England, Eastern Waterfan is the only one that lives in water rather than on soil, rocks, or trees in terrestrial habitats.
Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has evenly-spaced, rounded lobes, alternating dog lichen has its distinctive alternating finger-like projections along the edges.
Among the pelt lichens, freckled pelt is the only one with distinctive dark green cephalodia (freckles), making identification fairly straightforward.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a smooth surface, peppered pelt is distinguished by its dark spotted pattern.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, sheepish pelt lichen is distinguished by its uniquely woolly surface texture - most other Peltigera species have smooth or slightly wrinkled surfaces.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a relatively uniform surface with veins on the underside, concentric pelt lichen displays obvious ring patterns on top.
Among the many pelt lichens in New England, field dog lichen stands out for its incredibly soft, velvety surface texture - most other dog lichens feel smoother or more leathery.
Carpet pelt lichen differs from its pelt lichen relatives by its consistently smooth upper surface and preference for soil rather than rocks or trees.

Among the many pelt lichen species in New England, membranous pelt lichen stands out for its distinctly thin, papery texture - much more delicate than the thicker, more leathery dog pelt lichen or scaly pelt lichen.
Unlike the smooth-surfaced dog pelt lichen or the powdery-edged freckled pelt lichen, mother-of-many pelt is immediately recognizable by its bumpy, phyllidia-covered surface.

Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has rounded, disk-like apothecia along the lobe edges, blacksaddle pelt has distinctive tubular, saddle-shaped reproductive structures on the lichen surface.

Compared to its Peltigera relatives, tree pelt lichen has a distinctly more velvety surface texture and tends to be more brownish in color than the grayer dog pelt lichen or the more distinctly veined fan pelt lichen.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, fan pelt lichen stands out with its smooth upper surface and distinctive raised black veins underneath.

Among pelt lichens, the pale-bellied pelt is distinguished by its consistently pale underside, whereas dog pelt lichen has a darker, often brownish underside with prominent veins, and freckled pelt lichen has distinctive dark spots on its upper surface.
